# Brann

## Personality

Gruff, watchful and proud of his city. He welcomes everyone and trusts nobody until they have earned it.

## Lore

Brann is forty-eight, Sergeant of the great gate of Selsior, and the first face most travellers see when they come in off the Royal Road. It is a gruff face, weathered and watchful, and it does not smile until it has decided to. "Welcome to Selsior," he tells everyone who comes through, and he means it. "Keep to the road and mind the Guard," he adds, and he means that too.

### The gate is his

Brann joined the Royal Guard at nineteen, twenty-nine years ago, and he has stood at the gate for twenty of those years and commanded it for the last twelve. He has never wanted to be anywhere else. Other guards dream of the road patrol or the Knights' Court; Brann has always thought the gate was the most important post in the city, because it is where Selsior meets everyone else. Every envoy, carter, pilgrim, performer and adventurer who comes to the capital along the Royal Road passes under his eye, and he is fiercely proud of what they find on the other side.

He is proud of the city in the way some people are proud of a family. He will tell any traveller who stands still long enough that Selsior has stood since before the roads were laid, that it grew out of the field where the treaty was signed, and that there is nothing on Veligor you cannot find inside its walls if you look long enough. He welcomes everyone. He trusts nobody until they have earned it. He sees no contradiction in this, and after twenty years at the gate, neither do most of his guards.

### The people at the gate

Hollis, one of his gate guards, stands twelve hours a day at the gate and still likes looking out over the Royal Road. He starts every greeting stern, the way Brann taught him, and ends it smiling, which Brann did not. Brann grumbles about it and has never once told him to stop, because travellers like Hollis, and a gate that travellers like is a gate that hears things.

Swithin, the gate clerk, has written down everyone who came and went since before Brann was a recruit. The two of them are old colleagues and, though neither would put it so, old friends: Brann watches the faces, Swithin keeps the names, and between them very little gets past the gate that they do not know about. Swithin imagines adventures for every traveller in his book. Brann pretends to find this ridiculous and then asks what Swithin has written about the interesting ones.

And then there is Biscuit. The dog turned up at the gate four winters ago, thin and hopeful, and the guards never managed to send him away. Brann says he is keeping the dog because a gate needs a watchdog. Biscuit has never watched anything but a bread roll in his life. He sleeps by the gatehouse, follows his nose to the Crown Market every morning and comes back smelling of bread, and Brann, who trusts nobody, slips him the crusts off his own supper and thinks no one has noticed.

### Quiet, until it is not

Brann likes to say the road is quiet, until it is not. Lately it is not more often than it used to be. Swithin has noticed that fewer travellers come in on foot these days and more come in hurt, and Brann has noticed the same thing from the other end: more wagons riding in close together, more hired swords sitting on the tailboards, more caravans like Merrick's that pay well for guards because they have to. When a traveller comes in limping, Brann sends them to an apothecary first and asks his questions after, and he passes what he hears to the Knights' Court the same day.

### What he wants and fears

Brann wants the gate to stay what it has always been: open, busy and safe. What he fears is the day he has to close it in daylight.

A quest might begin with a traveller who comes through the gate without appearing in Swithin's book, or with Biscuit refusing, for the first time anyone can remember, to go out onto the road.
